# 12-Week Postpartum Return Programme

**Client profile:** 33-year-old female, 4 weeks post uncomplicated C-section, cleared for light activity only until 6-week OB check-up. Training environment: home, yoga mat only.

## Important Caveats Before You Begin

- **Do not progress past Phase 1 without OB clearance at her 6-week check.** If clearance is delayed or restricted, hold her at Phase 1.
- **Screen for diastasis recti** before any abdominal loading (week 5 onward). A simple supine knee-bent check works: more than 2 finger-widths separation along the linea alba warrants a referral to a pelvic floor physiotherapist before progressing core work.
- **Watch the C-section scar.** Any pulling, sharp pain, redness, or discharge — stop and refer back to her doctor. Scar massage can begin once fully healed and she's comfortable (usually 6–8 weeks, with OB sign-off).
- **Symptoms to stop immediately:** heavy bleeding return, pelvic heaviness/bulging (prolapse signs), urinary leakage, abdominal doming/coning, scar pain.
- **Sleep, feeding demands, and emotional state will dictate intensity more than the programme will.** Build flexibility in — if she's had a rough night, swap a session for a walk and breathwork.
- A pelvic floor physiotherapist referral early in the process is strongly recommended; this programme assumes she has access to one or that you've screened her adequately.

---

## PHASE 1 — Foundation & Reconnection (Weeks 1–2 of programme / Weeks 4–6 postpartum)

**Goal:** Gentle reactivation of breath, pelvic floor, and deep core. Walking volume. No abdominal flexion, no loaded movement, no impact.

### Weekly structure
- 5–6 days/week of walking
- 5 days/week of breath + pelvic floor work (10–15 min, can be split)

### Week 1
**Walking:** 15–20 min, flat, easy conversational pace. Daily if tolerated.

**Daily breath & floor session (10 min):**
- Diaphragmatic breathing, supine knees bent — 5 min, slow nasal inhale expanding ribs 360°, long exhale
- Pelvic floor connection on exhale (gentle "lift" — think stopping wind and urine flow lightly) — 2 sets of 10 slow contractions, full release between each
- Supported side-lying rest with deep breathing — 3 min

### Week 2
**Walking:** 20–30 min daily. Introduce one slightly longer walk (35 min) on a good day.

**Daily session (12–15 min):**
- Diaphragmatic breathing — 3 min
- Pelvic floor: 2 × 10 slow holds (3–5 sec), plus 2 × 10 quick flicks
- Add: supine pelvic tilts — 2 × 10 (no crunching)
- Add: glute bridges, slow, exhale up — 2 × 8
- Cat-cow on all fours — 2 × 8

**END OF WEEK 2 — 6-WEEK OB CHECK.** Do not progress without clearance.

---

## PHASE 2 — Rebuild Foundations (Weeks 3–5 / Weeks 7–9 postpartum)

**Goal:** Reintroduce light strength work, bodyweight only. Continue floor and breath work. Still no crunches/sit-ups, no planks yet, no impact.

### Weekly structure
- 3 strength sessions (25–30 min)
- 3–4 walks (30–45 min)
- Daily floor/breath work, 5 min

### Week 3 — Strength Session A (M/W/F)
Warm-up: cat-cow ×8, glute bridge ×10, diaphragmatic breath ×5

1. Glute bridge — 3 × 10, exhale on the lift
2. Bodyweight squat to chair/sofa height — 3 × 10
3. Bird dog — 3 × 6/side, slow, no hip rocking
4. Wall push-up — 3 × 8
5. Dead bug, heel taps only (one foot stays planted) — 2 × 6/side, no abdominal doming
6. Side-lying clamshell — 2 × 10/side

Cool-down: child's pose, supine knee hugs, breathwork — 3 min

### Week 4 — same template, progress as follows
- Squats: 3 × 12
- Glute bridge: add a 2-sec pause at top, 3 × 10
- Bird dog: 3 × 8/side
- Wall push-up: 3 × 10
- Dead bug heel taps: 2 × 8/side
- Add: side-lying leg lifts — 2 × 10/side

### Week 5
- Squats: 3 × 15
- Single-leg glute bridge (if pelvis stays level) — 3 × 6/side
- Bird dog with 2-sec hold — 3 × 8/side
- Incline push-up (hands on sofa) — 3 × 8
- Dead bug, opposite arm + heel tap — 2 × 8/side
- Clamshells with pulse — 2 × 12/side

**Diastasis re-check at end of Week 5.** If any doming during dead bug or bridges, regress.

---

## PHASE 3 — Build Strength & Capacity (Weeks 6–9 / Weeks 10–13 postpartum)

**Goal:** Progress load via tempo, range, and unilateral work. Begin gentle low-impact conditioning. Reintroduce trunk work carefully.

### Weekly structure
- 3 strength sessions (35–40 min)
- 2 conditioning/walk sessions
- 1 mobility/recovery session
- 1 full rest day

### Session A — Lower body & core (Mon)
1. Goblet squat (use a heavy household item — water jug, weighted bag) — 3 × 10
2. Reverse lunge — 3 × 8/side
3. Single-leg glute bridge — 3 × 8/side
4. Bird dog — 3 × 10/side
5. Dead bug, full (opposite arm + leg extend) — 3 × 6/side
6. Side plank from knees — 2 × 15 sec/side

### Session B — Upper body & posterior chain (Wed)
1. Incline push-up — 3 × 10
2. Floor row with towel/band (if available) or prone Y-T-W — 3 × 10
3. Hip hinge / Romanian deadlift bodyweight, focus on form — 3 × 10
4. Wall sit — 3 × 20 sec
5. Standing pelvic floor work: slow contractions while holding wall sit
6. Bird dog crawl progression — 2 × 6/side

### Session C — Full body circuit (Fri)
Continuous, 3 rounds, 30 sec work / 30 sec rest:
- Bodyweight squat
- Incline push-up
- Reverse lunge (alternate)
- Glute bridge
- Side plank knees (switch sides each round)
- Standing march in place

### Conditioning (Tue/Thu)
- Brisk walks 40–50 min, include 4–6 × 1 min slightly faster pace intervals
- Or stair walking if she has stairs at home

### Weekly progression (Weeks 6 → 9)
- Wk 6: foundation reps as above
- Wk 7: +2 reps on each lift, side plank to 20 sec
- Wk 8: side plank to full (off knees) 2 × 15 sec, push-ups lower incline
- Wk 9: introduce tempo (3-sec lowering on squats, push-ups); side plank 2 × 25 sec

**End of Week 9: pelvic floor and impact-readiness check.** Before any running or jumping:
- No leakage during exertion
- No pelvic heaviness
- Can perform single-leg balance 30 sec, single-leg glute bridge 20 reps/side, walking lunge with control
- Can run on the spot 1 min symptom-free

If she fails these — stay low-impact. Refer to pelvic health physio if not already done.

---

## PHASE 4 — Reintroduce Impact & Load (Weeks 10–12 / Weeks 14–16 postpartum)

**Goal:** Gradual return to impact, full-range strength, and self-sustaining training. By the end, she should be confident progressing on her own or moving to your regular programming.

### Weekly structure
- 3 strength sessions (40 min)
- 2 conditioning sessions (one low-impact, one with light impact)
- 1 mobility session
- 1 rest day

### Week 10
**Strength A (lower-focused):**
1. Goblet squat — 4 × 8
2. Split squat — 3 × 8/side
3. Single-leg RDL — 3 × 6/side
4. Hip thrust off sofa — 3 × 10
5. Dead bug, weighted (hold object overhead) — 3 × 8/side
6. Side plank, full — 3 × 20 sec/side

**Strength B (upper/posterior):**
1. Push-up (knees or full) — 4 × 6–8
2. Towel/band row — 4 × 10
3. Pike push-up against wall — 3 × 6
4. Superman holds — 3 × 20 sec
5. Bear crawl hold — 3 × 20 sec
6. Bird dog with row (if band) — 3 × 8/side

**Strength C (full body):**
3 rounds:
- Squat jump — 5 reps (FIRST IMPACT REINTRODUCTION — only if Phase 3 checks passed; otherwise hold at bodyweight squats)
- Push-up — 8
- Reverse lunge — 8/side
- Side plank with hip lift — 6/side
- Glute bridge march — 10/side

**Conditioning:** One low-impact walk 45 min; one walk-jog interval session: 5 × (1 min slow jog, 2 min walk), only if symptom-free.

### Week 11
- Add a rep or 5 sec to most exercises
- Walk-jog: 6 × (90 sec jog, 90 sec walk)
- Introduce light plyo: low box step-ups, skater steps (no jump yet)

### Week 12
- Strength: choose her strongest movements and test a tougher set — e.g. push-up AMRAP, longest side plank, max bodyweight squats in 60 sec. Use this as her baseline going forward.
- Conditioning: 20 min continuous jog/walk, aim for 10 min continuous jog if symptom-free
- Add: skater hops, low jumps 2 × 8 reps if no symptoms

---

## Nutrition & Recovery Notes

The trainer didn't ask for nutrition but a few essentials worth flagging:

- **If breastfeeding,** she needs an additional ~400–500 kcal/day above maintenance and should not aggressively diet — milk supply and recovery suffer. Hydration is critical (3+ L/day if breastfeeding).
- **Protein:** target ~1.6 g/kg bodyweight/day to support tissue repair and lean mass maintenance.
- **Iron, omega-3, vitamin D, and continued prenatal/postnatal vitamin** are typically recommended postpartum — refer to her GP/OB for bloods if she feels persistently fatigued (rule out anaemia and thyroid issues, which are common postpartum).
- **Sleep is the dominant recovery variable** and will be compromised. Frame the programme around what she can do, not what's "optimal."
- **Mental health check-ins:** postnatal depression and anxiety affect ~1 in 7. If mood, motivation, or affect concerns you, refer back to her GP. Don't treat it as a training problem.

## Programme End

By week 12 she should have: reconnected core and pelvic floor function, full bodyweight strength foundation, tolerance to light impact, and the ability to progress into general strength or running programming. Reassess goals at this point — return to pre-pregnancy training, postnatal fitness goals, or a specific event — and build the next block around her direction.

# Breastfeeding-Supportive Nutrition Plan

**To run alongside the 12-week training programme.**

## Important Caveats Before You Use This

- **Stay in your scope.** As a trainer, you can provide general nutrition guidance and healthy eating principles. If she has specific medical concerns (low milk supply, gestational diabetes history, allergies, suspected postnatal depression affecting eating, disordered eating history), refer to a registered dietitian or her GP.
- **No aggressive deficits while breastfeeding.** Weight loss is a likely goal, but rapid fat loss can suppress milk supply and tank her energy. The plan below is set at maintenance-to-slight-surplus for the early phase, easing toward a small deficit only in Phase 3–4 if she wants it.
- **She should be working with her GP/midwife on supplementation.** Most postnatal guidance includes continuing a prenatal/postnatal multivitamin throughout breastfeeding.

---

## Energy Needs

Breastfeeding burns roughly **400–500 kcal/day** producing milk (more in the first 6 months of exclusive feeding, less as solids are introduced around month 6).

**Working estimates** (adjust to her actual stats — ask for height, weight, activity level):

For a 33-year-old woman, ~65–70 kg, training 4–5x/week:
- Maintenance (non-lactating): ~2,000–2,200 kcal
- **Maintenance while breastfeeding (Phase 1–2): ~2,400–2,600 kcal**
- **Small deficit if desired (Phase 3–4): ~2,200–2,400 kcal**

**Do not drop below ~1,800 kcal/day while exclusively breastfeeding.** Milk supply and her recovery will suffer.

**Red flags she's under-eating:** drop in milk supply, persistent fatigue beyond what sleep deprivation explains, dizziness, mood crash, hair loss beyond normal postpartum shedding, loss of period not returning.

## Macronutrient Targets

Based on ~70 kg bodyweight, adjust proportionally:

- **Protein: 1.6–1.8 g/kg = 110–125 g/day.** Critical for tissue repair (C-section healing), lean mass, and satiety. Lactation itself doesn't massively increase protein needs, but training + recovery does.
- **Carbohydrates: 4–5 g/kg = 280–350 g/day.** Lactation is glucose-hungry. Low-carb dieting while breastfeeding is a bad idea — it tanks supply and energy.
- **Fat: 70–90 g/day.** Include omega-3 sources; DHA passes into breastmilk and supports infant brain development.
- **Fibre: 25–30 g/day.** Postpartum constipation is common, especially post-C-section and with iron supplementation.

## Hydration

- **3–3.5 L of fluid per day** while exclusively breastfeeding.
- Easy rule: a full glass of water at every feed plus regular sipping. Urine should be pale straw colour.
- Caffeine: up to ~200–300 mg/day is generally considered safe while breastfeeding (~2 cups of coffee). Watch for infant fussiness/sleep disruption.
- Alcohol: if she chooses to drink, the rule of thumb is one standard drink, timed after a feed, with 2+ hours before the next feed.

## Key Micronutrients for Breastfeeding

Cover these via food primarily, supplement to fill gaps:

- **Iodine** — 290 µg/day. Often under-consumed. Sources: dairy, eggs, white fish, iodised salt. Most postnatal multis contain it.
- **Vitamin D** — 10 µg (400 IU)/day minimum, often more. Recommended throughout breastfeeding.
- **Omega-3 (DHA)** — 200–300 mg/day. Oily fish 2x/week or an algae/fish oil supplement.
- **Iron** — postpartum iron stores are often low, especially post-surgery and with blood loss. Red meat, lentils, dark leafy greens, fortified cereals. Pair plant sources with vitamin C. If she's exhausted beyond the expected, ask her GP for ferritin bloods.
- **Calcium** — 1,000 mg/day. Bone density takes a hit during lactation; this matters.
- **B12** — especially if vegetarian/vegan, supplementation is essential.
- **Choline** — eggs are the easiest source; important for infant brain development.

## Meal Structure & Practical Framework

She has a newborn. The plan needs to survive sleep deprivation and one-handed eating. Build around:

**4 meals + 2 snacks**, all designed to be eaten cold, one-handed if needed, and prepped in batches.

### Daily template (~2,500 kcal)

**Breakfast (~550 kcal)**
- 3 eggs scrambled + 2 slices wholegrain toast + ½ avocado + handful spinach
- Or: Greek yoghurt bowl — 250 g full-fat Greek yoghurt + 50 g oats + berries + 1 tbsp peanut butter + 1 tbsp seeds

**Mid-morning snack (~300 kcal)**
- Apple + 30 g cheese + handful almonds
- Or: protein shake (30 g whey/plant) + banana

**Lunch (~600 kcal)**
- 150 g chicken/salmon/tofu + 1 cup cooked rice or quinoa + large mixed salad + olive oil dressing
- Or: wholegrain wrap with 150 g protein, hummus, greens, peppers + side of fruit

**Afternoon snack (~300 kcal)**
- 2 oatcakes + cottage cheese + tomato
- Or: smoothie — milk, banana, oats, peanut butter, protein powder

**Dinner (~600 kcal)**
- 150 g lean beef/salmon/chicken + roasted sweet potato + 2 cups roasted vegetables + olive oil
- Or: lentil & vegetable curry with brown rice + Greek yoghurt

**Evening snack (~150 kcal)** — especially if doing night feeds
- Banana + glass of milk
- Or: small bowl of porridge

### Hydration scaffolding
- 500 ml water on waking
- Glass of water at each feed (×8–12/day = ~2 L through feeds alone)
- Herbal teas, milk, soups all count

## Phase-by-Phase Adjustments

### Phase 1 (Weeks 1–2 of programme / 4–6 weeks postpartum)
- **Energy: ~2,500–2,600 kcal.** No deficit. She's healing from surgery.
- **Emphasise:** protein at every meal, healing nutrients (vitamin C, zinc, protein for wound repair), iron-rich foods, fibre and fluid for constipation.
- **Practical priority:** batch cook now or get help. Freezer meals, slow cooker meals, easy snacks within arm's reach of feeding stations.

### Phase 2 (Weeks 3–5 / 7–9 weeks postpartum)
- **Energy: ~2,400–2,500 kcal.** Still at maintenance.
- Bump protein slightly with training load increase — aim 120 g+/day.
- Add a post-training snack: 20–30 g protein + carbs within 60 min of strength sessions. Examples: chocolate milk, Greek yoghurt + fruit, protein shake + banana.

### Phase 3 (Weeks 6–9 / 10–13 weeks postpartum)
- **If fat loss is a goal AND milk supply is established AND she feels energetic: introduce a small deficit, ~2,200–2,300 kcal.** Otherwise hold at maintenance.
- Target weight loss if dieting: **maximum 0.5 kg/week.** Faster than this risks supply.
- Monitor milk supply weekly. Signs of drop: fewer wet nappies in baby (<6/day), fussiness at breast, baby weight gain slowing. If any appear, return to maintenance immediately.
- Pre/post training nutrition becomes more important — don't train fasted in this phase.

### Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12 / 14–16 weeks postpartum)
- Continue Phase 3 approach, or return to maintenance if she's hit her goal or supply concerns appear.
- Pre-impact training: she needs adequate fuel before walk-jog and plyo sessions. A small carb + protein snack 60–90 min before is ideal.

## Supplements Worth Discussing (with her GP)

- **Postnatal multivitamin** — continue throughout breastfeeding
- **Vitamin D** — 10 µg/day minimum (most prenatals cover this)
- **Omega-3 (DHA)** — 200–300 mg/day
- **Iron** — only if bloods confirm deficiency; not casually supplemented
- **Magnesium glycinate** in the evening — may help with sleep quality and constipation; safe while breastfeeding

**Skip:** "lactation cookies" and most "milk-boosting" herbal supplements (fenugreek, blessed thistle) — evidence is weak and some can affect supply negatively or interact with conditions. Supply is best supported by frequent feeding, hydration, calories, and sleep.

## What to Avoid or Minimise

- **Crash dieting / skipping meals** — supply and mood casualties.
- **Very low-carb / keto** — incompatible with lactation energy demands.
- **High-mercury fish** — limit swordfish, marlin, shark, king mackerel. Salmon, sardines, trout are excellent.
- **Excess alcohol and caffeine.**
- **Restrictive elimination diets** without a clinical reason — if she suspects baby has a food intolerance via breastmilk, refer to GP/dietitian rather than guessing.

## Monitoring & Adjustment

Have her track weekly:
- **Bodyweight** — once a week, same day, same time. Not daily.
- **Energy levels (1–10)**
- **Milk supply confidence (1–10)** — or baby wet nappies/day if she's tracking
- **Mood and sleep quality**
- **Training performance** — is she progressing or stalling?

If energy, supply, or mood drop for **two consecutive weeks**, add 200–300 kcal back in (mostly carbs) and reassess.

## When to Refer Out

- Suspected low supply → lactation consultant
- Persistent fatigue beyond newborn-normal → GP for bloods (iron, thyroid, vitamin D)
- Disordered eating patterns or extreme weight-loss focus → GP / registered dietitian
- Mood concerns → GP (postnatal depression screening)
- Specific nutritional needs (vegan, allergies, gestational diabetes history) → registered dietitian

---

This plan is deliberately conservative on the deficit side. The goal across these 12 weeks is **a strong, well-fuelled, recovering mother with established milk supply** — not rapid fat loss. If she has aesthetic goals beyond this window, those become realistic to chase in months 6–12 postpartum, especially as breastfeeding demands decrease with the introduction of solids.

# Progressive Strength Programming — Phases 3 & 4 Expanded

The original Phase 3 and 4 sessions were appropriate for someone with no equipment, but they undersell what's possible — even at home, even with minimal kit. Here's an upgraded strength progression with proper loading, periodisation, and equipment recommendations.

## Equipment Recommendations

Before Phase 3 starts (end of week 5), ask her to invest in or borrow:

- **Resistance bands** — a set of loop bands (light/medium/heavy) and a long tube band with handles. ~£15–30.
- **Adjustable dumbbells** — ideal 2–24 kg range. ~£100–200. If budget is tight, a pair each of 5 kg, 8 kg, and 12 kg covers most needs.
- **A backpack** — load with books, rice bags, water bottles for weighted carries and squats. Free.
- **A sturdy chair, sofa, or low stool** — for split squats, step-ups, incline push-ups. Already has.
- **A door anchor** for the long band — opens up rows and pulldowns. ~£5.

If she'll only commit to **one purchase**: a set of resistance bands with a door anchor. Two purchases: add adjustable dumbbells.

---

## PHASE 3 — Build Strength & Capacity (Weeks 6–9 / 10–13 weeks postpartum)

**Strength training principle:** This is a true rebuilding block. Use bodyweight + bands + light dumbbells. Progress via **load, then reps, then tempo, then range.** Track loads each session.

**Volume guideline:** 3 strength sessions/week, ~40 min each.

### Session A — Lower Body (Monday)

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Goblet squat (DB or backpack) | 3 × 10 | Start light, focus on depth and breathing |
| Romanian deadlift (DBs) | 3 × 10 | Hip hinge, neutral spine |
| Reverse lunge (DBs at sides) | 3 × 8/side | Step back, control descent |
| Glute bridge with band above knees | 3 × 12 | Drive knees out |
| Dead bug, opposite arm + heel tap | 3 × 8/side | No doming |
| Side plank from knees | 2 × 20 sec/side | Progress to full as able |

### Session B — Upper Body & Posterior Chain (Wednesday)

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Incline push-up (sofa/bench) | 3 × 10 | Lower the incline as strength returns |
| Band row (door anchor) | 3 × 12 | Squeeze shoulder blades, exhale on pull |
| DB shoulder press, seated | 3 × 10 | Avoid arching low back |
| Single-arm DB row (knee on sofa) | 3 × 10/side | Brace core, no rotation |
| Band pull-apart | 3 × 15 | Posture work |
| Bird dog | 3 × 10/side | Hold 2 sec at top |

### Session C — Full Body & Conditioning (Friday)

Circuit format, 3–4 rounds, 40 sec work / 20 sec rest:

- Goblet squat
- Incline push-up
- DB Romanian deadlift
- Band row
- Glute bridge with band
- Bear crawl hold or dead bug

### Week-by-week progression

**Week 6 — Introduction**
- Light loads, learn the patterns. Squat with 8 kg, RDL with 2×5 kg, press with 2×3–5 kg.
- Last 2 reps of each set should feel like there are 4–5 more in the tank (RPE 5–6).

**Week 7 — Load**
- Add 1–2 kg to compound lifts where form is solid.
- Same rep schemes. RPE 6–7 by end of set.

**Week 8 — Volume**
- Add a set to the main lifts: Squat 4 × 10, RDL 4 × 10, Row 4 × 12.
- Maintain Week 7 loads.

**Week 9 — Tempo & test**
- Introduce tempo: 3-second lowering phase on squats, RDLs, push-ups, presses. This drives strength without needing heavier weights.
- End of week: note her working loads. These are her baseline going into Phase 4.

### Phase 3 strength targets (end of Week 9, ~70 kg client)
- Goblet squat: 12–16 kg × 10 reps
- DB RDL: 2 × 10–12 kg × 10 reps
- DB row: 10–14 kg × 10 reps/side
- Incline push-up at lower incline (e.g. coffee table) × 10
- Full side plank × 25 sec/side
- Single-leg glute bridge × 10/side

If she's well behind these, hold Phase 3 for another week or two before progressing.

---

## PHASE 4 — Reintroduce Impact & Build Strength (Weeks 10–12 / 14–16 weeks postpartum)

**Strength training principle:** Move from rebuild to genuine strength development. Lower rep ranges on main lifts, introduce unilateral loading, add deliberate plyometric progression. This is where she starts to feel strong again.

**Volume guideline:** 3 strength sessions/week, ~45 min each. Add **deliberate warm-up sets** to main lifts now.

### Session A — Lower Body Strength (Monday)

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Loading guide |
|---|---|---|
| Goblet squat | 4 × 8 | Heavier — RPE 7 |
| DB Romanian deadlift | 4 × 8 | Heaviest available DBs |
| Bulgarian split squat (rear foot on sofa) | 3 × 8/side | DBs at sides |
| Hip thrust off sofa (DB on hips) | 3 × 10 | Squeeze hard at top |
| Suitcase carry (single DB) | 3 × 30 sec/side | Heavy — anti-lateral flexion core work |
| Side plank with hip dip | 3 × 8/side | Full side plank position |

### Session B — Upper Body Strength (Wednesday)

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Push-up (full or knees) | 4 × 6–10 | Aim to progress from knee to full this phase |
| Single-arm DB row | 4 × 8/side | Heavier than Phase 3 |
| DB shoulder press, standing | 4 × 8 | Standing brings core in |
| Band-resisted floor press or DB floor press | 3 × 10 | Horizontal pressing |
| Band face pull | 3 × 15 | Rear delts and posture |
| Pallof press (band at door anchor) | 3 × 10/side | Anti-rotation core |

### Session C — Power & Full Body (Friday)

This session introduces plyometrics and is **conditional on passing the impact readiness check** at the end of Phase 3.

**Power block** (skip jumps if any pelvic floor symptoms — substitute with bodyweight squats and step-ups):
- Bodyweight squat jump or low box step-up — 4 × 5
- Skater hops (lateral) or lateral step-out — 4 × 6/side
- Med ball slam or hard exhale push-up — 4 × 5

**Strength block** (3 rounds):
- Goblet squat × 10
- DB row × 10/side
- Reverse lunge × 8/side
- DB shoulder press × 8
- Farmer's carry × 40 sec

### Week-by-week progression

**Week 10 — Introduction to lower reps**
- Main lifts at 4 × 8 with loads that feel like RPE 7 by final set.
- Introduce 1 power exercise on Session C: low squat jumps × 5, 3 sets only. Watch for symptoms.

**Week 11 — Load**
- Add load to compound lifts. Goblet squat aiming for 16–20 kg, RDL 2 × 14–16 kg.
- Power: 2 plyo exercises now — squat jumps + skater hops. 4 × 5 each.
- Add a rep to upper body work: push-ups 4 × 8–10.

**Week 12 — Test & consolidate**
- Test her working strength on key lifts. For each main movement, work up to a top set of 6 reps at RPE 8 (2 reps left in tank).
- Document: top goblet squat × 6, top RDL × 6, top row × 6, max push-ups in a set, longest side plank, max consecutive squat jumps symptom-free.
- These become her baseline for the next training block.

### Phase 4 strength targets (end of Week 12, ~70 kg client)
- Goblet squat: 18–24 kg × 8 reps
- DB RDL: 2 × 14–18 kg × 8 reps
- Bulgarian split squat: 2 × 8–10 kg × 8/side
- DB row: 12–16 kg × 8/side
- DB shoulder press: 2 × 7–10 kg × 8
- Push-up: 8–10 full reps
- Hip thrust: 20+ kg × 10
- 5 consecutive squat jumps symptom-free

---

## How to Apply Progressive Overload

Each week, she should be doing **one** of these on at least the main lifts:

1. **More weight** at same reps (preferred)
2. **More reps** at same weight
3. **Slower tempo** at same weight/reps
4. **Better range of motion** at same load
5. **An extra set** if reps and load have stalled

Do not progress all variables at once. Pick one per lift per week. If she had a bad night's sleep or feels off, **repeat the previous week** — don't push.

## Symptom Monitoring During Strength Work

Continue watching for the original red flags throughout strength progression:

- **Abdominal doming/coning** during any lift → regress the exercise, drop load, re-check diastasis
- **Pelvic heaviness, leakage, bulging** → stop the movement immediately, reduce intensity, refer to pelvic floor physio
- **Scar pulling or pain** → reduce range, stop the exercise, refer to GP if persistent
- **Breath holding** — she should be exhaling on exertion (the "blow before you go" cue). Breath-holding under load increases intra-abdominal pressure, which is what we're avoiding while the abdominal wall and pelvic floor rebuild.

## Nutrition Integration

As loads climb in Phase 4, her training demand increases. Re-check:

- **Protein intake** — she should be consistently hitting 120–130 g/day. Add a post-training protein source within an hour of strength sessions.
- **Carb intake before training** — at least 30–40 g carbs in the 60–90 min before Session A and C.
- **Energy availability** — if she's in the small deficit from the nutrition plan and strength stalls for 2 weeks running, return to maintenance. You cannot out-program under-eating, especially while breastfeeding.

## What Comes After Week 12

End of Week 12 she should have:
- A working strength base across all major patterns (squat, hinge, push, pull, carry, anti-rotation)
- Tolerance to light plyometrics
- Confidence with her body again

**Next block options** to discuss with her:
1. **Continued strength block** — push toward heavier dumbbells, introduce barbell work if she'll join a gym, target specific strength benchmarks
2. **Return to running** — structured couch-to-5k style progression, with strength maintained 2x/week
3. **Hybrid training** — strength 2x/week, conditioning 2x/week, mobility 1x/week
4. **Specific goal block** — first pull-up, first push-up unbroken set of 10, postnatal-specific event

Reassess pelvic floor function, diastasis, and overall recovery before launching the next block. By 4 months postpartum she's still recovering — but she's also ready to train properly again.

# Returning to Abdominal Training Post-C-Section

This is the question every postpartum client asks, and it deserves a careful answer. The short version: she's already doing core work from Week 1 of the programme — it just doesn't look like the "abs work" she's picturing. Traditional crunches and sit-ups come much later, and some exercises (and expectations) need a frank conversation.

## The Honest Conversation to Have With Her First

Before you programme anything, set expectations. Three points worth raising:

**1. Her core is already being trained.** Diaphragmatic breathing, dead bugs, bird dogs, side planks, Pallof presses, suitcase carries — all of these are core training, and arguably better core training than crunches. The deep core (transverse abdominis, pelvic floor, diaphragm, multifidus) is the foundation. Without it, surface abs work is built on sand.

**2. "Getting her core back" is partly a body composition question, not a training one.** Visible abs require low body fat. While breastfeeding and recovering, aggressive fat loss is off the table. The nutrition plan reflects that. She can build genuine core strength now; visible definition will follow as feeding demands decrease and a sustainable deficit becomes appropriate.

**3. C-section recovery is different.** The abdominal wall was surgically incised — through skin, fascia, and (depending on technique) the rectus sheath. Scar tissue, altered nerve sensation, and weaker fascial integrity persist for **6–12 months**. The "mummy tummy" pooch above the scar is partly scar adhesion and fascial laxity, not just fat. It improves with time, scar mobilisation, and properly progressed core work — not with crunches.

If she has **diastasis recti** (abdominal separation), aggressive flexion-based abs work can make it worse. Always screen first.

## Diastasis Recti Screen (Do This Before Any Progression)

Have her lie supine, knees bent, feet flat. She lifts her head and shoulders slightly off the mat. With fingers horizontal, palpate along the linea alba (midline) at three points: 2 cm above the navel, at the navel, and 2 cm below.

Assess two things:
- **Width:** how many finger-widths apart are the rectus muscles?
- **Depth/tension:** does the gap feel firm (good — fascia regenerating) or soft and squishy (still healing)?

**Findings and what to do:**

- **<2 fingers, firm:** Proceed with progression below.
- **2–3 fingers, firm:** Proceed cautiously. Avoid flexion-based work until closer to 2.
- **>3 fingers OR soft/squishy at any width:** Refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist before progressing flexion-based core work. Continue deep core training only.
- **Doming or coning** during the test (a ridge popping up along the midline): stop, regress, refer.

Re-screen every 3–4 weeks. Almost all women have some diastasis at 6 weeks postpartum; the majority close significantly by 8 weeks, and most by 6 months.

## The Phased Return to Abdominal Training

### Phase 1 (Weeks 1–2 / 4–6 weeks postpartum) — Deep Core Reconnection

**Already in the programme.** This IS core work:
- Diaphragmatic breathing
- Pelvic floor connection on exhale
- Pelvic tilts
- Glute bridges (the exhale engages the deep core)

**Avoid:** crunches, sit-ups, planks, leg lifts, oblique twists, anything that creates intra-abdominal pressure.

**Cue:** "Connect, then move." On every exhale before a movement, gentle pelvic floor lift and lower abdominal draw-in. This becomes automatic by the end of Phase 2.

---

### Phase 2 (Weeks 3–5 / 7–9 weeks postpartum) — Anti-Movement Core

**Already in the programme.** All of these train the abs without flexion or pressure spikes:
- Dead bug, heel taps → opposite arm + heel tap → full
- Bird dog, progressing to holds
- Glute bridges, progressing to single-leg
- Side-lying clamshells and leg lifts

**Now add (Week 4–5 if diastosis screen is clean):**
- **Side plank from knees** — 2 × 15–20 sec/side. This is an oblique exercise, but a safe one — no flexion, builds lateral stability.
- **Bear hold** (hands and knees, knees hover 2 inches off floor) — 2 × 15 sec. Deep core under load.

**Still avoid:** crunches, sit-ups, full planks, V-sits, Russian twists, hanging leg raises, ab wheel.

---

### Phase 3 (Weeks 6–9 / 10–13 weeks postpartum) — Anti-Movement Loading

**Already in the programme, but let's expand the abs-specific work:**

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | What it trains |
|---|---|---|
| Dead bug, full opposite limb | 3 × 8/side | Anti-extension, deep core |
| Bird dog with 2-sec hold | 3 × 10/side | Anti-rotation, deep core |
| Side plank, full (off knees) | 3 × 20–30 sec/side | Lateral chain, obliques |
| Bear crawl hold | 3 × 20 sec | Whole core under load |
| Pallof press (band, kneeling then standing) | 3 × 10/side | Anti-rotation, obliques |
| Suitcase carry (single DB) | 3 × 30 sec/side | Anti-lateral flexion |

**Introduce around Week 8 (if diastasis is closed to <2 fingers, firm, no doming):**

- **Full plank from feet** — 3 × 15–20 sec, watching closely for doming or sagging. If either occurs, regress to incline plank (hands on sofa).
- **Hollow body hold, regressed** — knees bent, arms at sides, low back pressed into floor — 3 × 15 sec. This is the gateway to flexion-tolerant work.

**Still avoid:** sit-ups, crunches, hanging leg raises, ab wheel rollouts, Russian twists with weight, V-sits.

---

### Phase 4 (Weeks 10–12 / 14–16 weeks postpartum) — Reintroducing Flexion (Carefully)

**This is the earliest she should be doing crunch-pattern work, and only if:**
- Diastasis is closed (<2 fingers, firm) or significantly improved with no doming
- No pelvic floor symptoms with current loading
- She's tolerating Phase 3 anti-movement work well
- Scar is fully healed, mobile, no pulling sensation

**Session C in Phase 4 already includes a power block. Add an abs finisher (5–8 min at the end of any session):**

**Week 10 — Reintroduce flexion gently**
- Heel slides with deep core engagement — 2 × 10
- Hollow body hold, progressed (legs straight, arms overhead) — 3 × 15–20 sec
- Side plank with hip dip — 3 × 8/side
- Pallof press with rotation — 3 × 8/side

**Week 11 — Add controlled flexion**
- Reverse crunch (knees to chest, slow, no momentum) — 3 × 8
- Hollow body rocks — 3 × 8
- Side plank with reach-through — 3 × 8/side
- Dead bug with band resistance — 3 × 10/side

**Week 12 — Build capacity**
- Bicycle crunches, slow and controlled — 3 × 10/side
- Hanging knee raise (if she has a bar) OR lying leg raise with low back pinned — 3 × 8
- Side plank with hip dip + reach — 3 × 8/side
- Plank with shoulder taps — 3 × 10/side

**Still avoid even at Week 12:**
- **Sit-ups** (full flexion to vertical) — high pressure, high diastasis risk, low value vs. alternatives
- **V-sits, jackknives** — same reason
- **Ab wheel rollouts** — too much demand on the linea alba this early
- **Weighted Russian twists** — combined rotation + load on a healing core is a bad bet
- **Heavy decline sit-ups** — no benefit, real risk

These can be considered from **6+ months postpartum** if everything has progressed well, but honestly, they're not necessary for a strong, defined core. Anti-movement work + carries + controlled flexion is more effective and far safer.

---

## C-Section Scar Considerations

**Scar mobilisation** can begin once the scar is fully healed and signed off by her OB (usually 6–8 weeks). Benefits: reduces adhesions, improves abdominal wall function, reduces the "shelf" appearance above the scar.

Simple protocol, 5 min/day:
1. **Touch and desensitise** — gentle finger pressure across the scar in all directions
2. **Skin rolling** — gently lift the skin above and below the scar between fingers
3. **Circular massage** — small circles directly on the scar with one or two fingers
4. **Stretch directions** — pull skin gently in each direction, hold 10 sec

If she has significant adhesion, numbness, pulling, or pain, refer to a women's health physio who does scar work — this is a specialist skill and worth the referral. Improvements in scar mobility often unlock progress in core function.

---

## Realistic Timeline & Expectations

Be honest with her:

- **By Week 12 of this programme (~4 months postpartum):** strong functional core, full plank, side planks, controlled flexion work. Pooch likely still present.
- **By 6 months postpartum:** if nutrition has supported a small fat loss phase, visible improvement. Core strength approaching pre-pregnancy.
- **By 9–12 months postpartum:** for most women who train consistently and have stopped or reduced breastfeeding, the abdominal wall has substantially recovered. Visible definition is achievable with a deliberate fat loss phase.
- **Permanent changes:** the scar will fade but remain. Some women retain a small fascial laxity above the scar regardless of training. This is normal and worth normalising for her.

**What makes the biggest difference long-term:**
1. Deep core function restored (months 1–4)
2. Progressive strength training across the whole body — not just abs (months 3–12)
3. Sustainable fat loss phase when breastfeeding allows (months 6–12+)
4. Scar mobility work (months 2–6)
5. Patience.

## Red Flags to Watch During Abs Progression

Stop and regress (or refer) if she develops:
- Doming or coning along the midline during any exercise
- Pelvic heaviness, pressure, or bulging
- Urinary leakage
- Lower back pain that wasn't there before
- Scar pain or pulling
- A sense that she "can't connect" to her core

These aren't reasons to push through — they're signals the load is ahead of her current capacity. Regress, reinforce the basics, and progress again when symptoms clear.

## The Core Programming Summary

| Phase | Weeks | What she does for abs |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1–2 | Breathing, pelvic floor, pelvic tilts |
| 2 | 3–5 | Dead bug, bird dog, side plank from knees, bear hold |
| 3 | 6–9 | Loaded anti-movement work, full plank, hollow body regressed |
| 4 | 10–12 | Reintroduce controlled flexion, side plank progressions, hollow body holds, reverse crunches |
| Beyond | 12+ | Standard core training, carries, eventually weighted flexion work if desired |

Tell her: the goal isn't to get back to doing 100 sit-ups. The goal is a core that's strong, functional, and looks the way she wants it to. The path there is slower than she'd like, but it's the only path that works.

# Phase 3 — Intensity Push

Good instinct on her part, and reasonable to act on if she's progressing well. **Before you push intensity, confirm the green-light criteria** — if any of these are off, hold the original Phase 3 and don't push harder.

## Green-Light Criteria (Confirm Before You Push)

All of these must be true at the start of Week 6:
- **Diastasis closed to <2 fingers, firm**, no doming on dead bug or bridges
- **No pelvic floor symptoms** — no leakage, no heaviness, no bulging
- **C-section scar fully healed, mobile, no pulling**
- **Sleep averaging 5+ hours total per night** (broken is fine)
- **Energy 6+/10 on most days**
- **Milk supply established and stable** (if breastfeeding)
- **Phase 2 sessions completed without symptom flare**
- **Nutrition at maintenance, not in deficit**

If any are off, run the original Phase 3 as written. Intensity built on a compromised foundation is how postpartum clients get hurt or develop symptoms that take months to resolve.

If she's green across the board, here's the upgraded block.

---

## What "Pushing Intensity" Means Here

It does **not** mean training to failure, max effort plyometrics, or heavy bilateral lifting under load. It means:

1. **Lower rep ranges on main lifts** (8–6 instead of 10–12) with heavier loads
2. **More sets** on key compounds
3. **Slower eccentrics** and pause work — drives strength without needing equipment she doesn't have
4. **Density** — shorter rest periods on accessory work
5. **Unilateral loading** progressed harder than the original Phase 3
6. **An optional 4th session** if she has the capacity

This is still postpartum-appropriate. We're pushing the ceiling of Phase 3, not skipping into Phase 4 work.

---

## Upgraded Phase 3 — Strength Block

**Frequency:** 3 sessions/week minimum, optional 4th. ~45 min each.

**Rest periods:** 90 sec on main lifts (up from 60), 45–60 sec on accessories.

**RPE targeting:** Main lifts at RPE 7–8 by Week 8 (2–3 reps left in the tank). Previously we held at RPE 6–7.

### Session A — Lower Body (Monday)

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Tempo / Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Goblet squat | 4 × 8 | 3-sec lowering, 1-sec pause at bottom |
| DB Romanian deadlift | 4 × 8 | 3-sec lowering, feel hamstrings load |
| Reverse lunge (DBs) | 3 × 8/side | Controlled, no momentum |
| Single-leg glute bridge | 3 × 10/side | 2-sec hold at top |
| Suitcase carry (heavy) | 3 × 40 sec/side | Anti-lateral flexion |
| Side plank, full | 3 × 25–30 sec/side | Add hip dip if easy |

### Session B — Upper Body & Posterior Chain (Wednesday)

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Tempo / Notes |

| Single-arm DB row | 4 × 8/side | Squeeze 1 sec at top |
| DB shoulder press, standing | 4 × 8 | Brace hard, no back arch |
| DB floor press | 3 × 10 | Horizontal pressing pattern |

This is a strength + density session, not a circuit. Pair exercises and move with purpose.

**Pair 1 (3 rounds, 60 sec rest after both done):**

## Week-by-Week Progression

The original Phase 3 had a gentle ramp. This one drives harder.

### Week 6 — Calibration
- Find working loads at the new rep ranges. Goblet squat should feel like RPE 7 by the final set of 8.
- Estimated starting loads: goblet squat 12–14 kg, RDL 2 × 8–10 kg, row 8–10 kg, press 2 × 5–7 kg.
- Tempo work in from day 1.
- **No 4th session this week.**

### Week 7 — Load
- Add weight where she finished Week 6 with reps in the tank.
- Squat aiming for 14–16 kg, RDL 2 × 10–12 kg, row 10–12 kg.
- Keep all tempo and rep schemes the same.
- **Optional 4th session in if recovery allows.**

### Week 8 — Density & volume
- Loads hold from Week 7. Reduce rest periods by 15 sec across the board.
- Add a set on main lifts: Squat 5 × 8, RDL 5 × 8, Row 5 × 8.
- This is the hardest week of the block.

### Week 9 — Peak & test
- Loads up again where possible: squat 16–20 kg, RDL 2 × 12–14 kg.
- Drop back to 4 × 8 (lower volume) but heavier.
- **End-of-week test session** (replace Session C):
  - Goblet squat: work up to a top set of 6 at RPE 8
  - Push-up: max unbroken reps with good form
  - Single-arm DB row: heaviest 8 reps/side
  - Side plank: longest hold/side
  - Suitcase carry: heaviest 40 sec/side
- Document everything. These numbers carry into Phase 4.

## Recovery Demands of the Pushed Block

You can't push intensity without paying for it in recovery. Non-negotiables while running this block:

- **Nutrition at maintenance, not deficit.** ~2,500 kcal, 130 g protein. The Phase 3 deficit suggestion in the nutrition plan is off the table here.
- **Pre-training fuel** before every session: 30–40 g carbs + 15–20 g protein, 60–90 min prior.
- **Post-training:** 30 g protein within an hour. Important on training days for both recovery and milk supply.
- **Hydration up:** 3.5 L/day minimum.
- **Sleep:** if she has a string of bad nights, replace Session D (and possibly Session C) with a walk and breathwork. This is non-negotiable. Training hard on no sleep while breastfeeding is how supply drops and injuries happen.
- **One full rest day per week, no walking either** — let her recover.

---

## Monitoring & Pull-Back Triggers

Weekly check at the end of each session, brief but real:

1. **Performance:** are loads/reps progressing, holding, or dropping?
2. **Energy (1–10):** trending where?
3. **Milk supply:** stable? Baby's nappies and feeding patterns normal?
4. **Symptoms:** any leakage, heaviness, doming, scar pulling, back pain?
5. **Sleep average over the week**
6. **Mood**

**Pull back to original Phase 3 immediately if:**
- Any diastasis doming returns
- Any pelvic floor symptom appears
- Milk supply drops noticeably
- Energy crashes for 3+ days
- Performance regresses for 2 weeks in a row
- Mood drops significantly (refer to GP if persistent)

Pulling back isn't failure. It's how she stays in training for the next decade rather than blowing up at 4 months postpartum and losing 6 weeks.

---

## The Honest Trade-off to Flag With Her

Pushing intensity in Phase 3 means:
- **More fatigue.** She'll feel it.
- **Higher symptom risk.** Especially if recovery slips.
- **Tighter margin for error** on nutrition, sleep, and screening.
- **No deficit phase** until at least Week 13+.

What she gets in return:
- Genuine strength gains by Week 12 — top sets at loads she'd have considered heavy pre-pregnancy
- A noticeably stronger, more capable body
- A solid base to push hard in months 5–12 postpartum

This is the right trade for a motivated client with good recovery support. It's the wrong trade for one who's running on three hours of sleep, exclusively feeding every two hours, and snapping at her partner. Read the room every week. The programme is the easy part — knowing when to push and when to hold is the job.

# Cardio Programming — 12-Week Postpartum Return

Cardio is already present in the original programme (walking from Day 1, walk-jog intervals in Phase 4) but it's been background to the strength work. Let's bring it forward as deliberate programming with proper progression and intent.

## Important Caveats First

- **Cardio is not a fat loss tool right now.** While breastfeeding and recovering, cardio is for cardiovascular health, energy, mood, and base-building for future running or athletic goals. The deficit needed for fat loss is off the table until at least Week 13+, and the nutrition plan caps it at 0.5 kg/week even then.
- **Impact comes late and only with clearance.** The Week 9 impact-readiness check is non-negotiable before any jogging, running, or jumping.
- **Pelvic floor dictates progression more than fitness does.** A cardio-fit client whose pelvic floor isn't ready will leak. That's the symptom telling you to hold.
- **High intensity has hormonal trade-offs.** Excessive HIIT while breastfeeding can affect milk supply and recovery. Volume and intensity must be balanced with feeding demands.
- **Heart rate is unreliable during breastfeeding.** Resting HR is elevated, recovery HR is variable, and HRV is affected. Use RPE (rate of perceived exertion) primarily. HR is a secondary data point at best.

## RPE Reference for Cardio

This is the primary tool throughout. Teach her this:

| RPE | What it feels like | Talking test |
|---|---|---|
| 3–4 | Easy, recovery pace | Full conversation, no pauses |
| 5–6 | Moderate, working | Full sentences, slight breath between |
| 7 | Hard but sustainable | Short sentences only |
| 8 | Hard, uncomfortable | Few words at a time |
| 9–10 | Very hard / max | Single words or none |

The vast majority of her cardio should sit at RPE 5–6. Higher intensities come in carefully, in small doses, late in the programme.

---

## PHASE 1 — Walking Base (Weeks 1–2 / 4–6 weeks postpartum)

**Goal:** Build daily walking habit. Aerobic base. Recovery support. No structured cardio beyond this.

| Week | Frequency | Session | RPE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Daily if tolerated | 15–20 min flat walk | 3 |
| 2 | Daily | 20–30 min flat walk, one 35 min on a good day | 3–4 |

**Notes:**
- Pram-pushing counts and is encouraged.
- Avoid hills, uneven terrain (early pelvic floor recovery handles flat better), and long durations on consecutive days early on.
- If she has lochia (postpartum bleeding) that increases after a walk, she's done too much. Pull back.
- **No structured intervals, no pace work, no incline.**

---

## PHASE 2 — Aerobic Base Building (Weeks 3–5 / 7–9 weeks postpartum)

**Goal:** Extend duration, introduce gentle variation, build aerobic capacity. Still no impact.

### Weekly cardio structure
- 3–4 walks of 30–45 min
- 1 longer walk of 45–60 min once a week
- All non-impact

### Week-by-week

**Week 3**
- 4 × 30–35 min walks at RPE 4
- 1 × 45 min walk at RPE 4
- Add: gentle incline (slight hill or treadmill 2–3%) on one walk

**Week 4**
- 4 × 35–40 min walks at RPE 4–5
- 1 × 50 min walk at RPE 4
- Introduce "pace play": during one walk, alternate 2 min normal pace / 1 min slightly brisker (RPE 5–6). 5 rounds.

**Week 5**
- 4 × 40 min walks at RPE 5
- 1 × 55–60 min walk at RPE 4
- Pace play: 4 min normal / 2 min brisk × 5

**Optional low-impact alternative if she has access:**
- Stationary bike at home: 25–35 min at RPE 5
- Swimming (only after 6-week OB check, lochia stopped, no infection) — 20–30 min easy
- These are excellent for cardio without any pelvic floor load.

### Pelvic floor cues during cardio
- Breathe diaphragmatically — don't chest-breathe under exertion
- No breath-holding on inclines
- If pelvic heaviness or leakage appears, slow down or shorten the walk
- Sports bra fit matters — engorged or post-feed breast size changes quickly. Recheck bra fit at Week 5 and again at Week 9.

---

## PHASE 3 — Conditioning Block (Weeks 6–9 / 10–13 weeks postpartum)

**Goal:** Real conditioning. Build the engine without impact. Prepare her cardiovascular system for the return to jogging in Phase 4.

### Weekly cardio structure
- 2 dedicated cardio sessions (separate from strength)
- Optional 3rd shorter session
- 1 long walk on the weekend

### Cardio Session 1 — Steady State (Tuesday)

| Week | Session | RPE |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 35 min brisk walk, include rolling incline | 5–6 |
| 7 | 40 min brisk walk with incline OR 30 min bike | 6 |
| 8 | 45 min brisk walk with incline OR 35 min bike | 6 |
| 9 | 30 min at RPE 6–7 (sustained effort) | 6–7 |

### Cardio Session 2 — Intervals (Thursday)

Low-impact intervals only. Use brisk walking, incline walking, bike, or hill walking.

| Week | Session |
|---|---|
| 6 | 5 min easy warm-up + 6 × (1 min RPE 7 / 2 min RPE 4) + 5 min cool-down |
| 7 | 5 min warm-up + 8 × (1 min RPE 7 / 90 sec RPE 4) + 5 min cool-down |
| 8 | 5 min warm-up + 6 × (90 sec RPE 7–8 / 90 sec RPE 4) + 5 min cool-down |
| 9 | 5 min warm-up + 5 × (2 min RPE 7–8 / 2 min RPE 4) + 5 min cool-down |

**What "RPE 7 work intervals" look like with no equipment:**
- Steep incline walking on treadmill
- Walking uphill at a brisk pace
- Bike at high resistance
- Step-ups on a sturdy box at pace (low impact, watch pelvic floor)
- Stair climbing — up at pace, walk back down

### Long walk (Saturday or Sunday)
- 60–75 min at RPE 4. This is base-building and recovery-friendly. Pram-pushing fine.

### Optional 3rd session (Saturday)
Only if recovery is good. Can replace with rest.
- 20–25 min easy bike or walk at RPE 4 — pure aerobic recovery

### What's deliberately missing in Phase 3
- **No jogging, no running, no jumping, no high-impact aerobics.** Tempting given her fitness will be returning, but the pelvic floor isn't yet ready to absorb impact forces under repeated load.
- **No max-effort intervals** (RPE 9–10). Top end of her intervals stays at RPE 7–8.

### Impact-Readiness Check (End of Week 9) — Reminder

Before any Phase 4 jogging, she must pass:
- No leakage during exertion or cough/sneeze
- No pelvic heaviness or bulging
- Single-leg balance × 30 sec each side
- Single-leg glute bridge × 20 reps/side
- Walking lunge with control
- 1 min jogging on the spot — symptom-free
- 10 single-leg hops/side — symptom-free
- 20 jumping jacks — symptom-free

**Fail any of these → no impact yet.** Stay on low-impact conditioning in Phase 4. This isn't being cautious for the sake of it — pelvic organ prolapse and stress incontinence developed at this stage can take months of physio to resolve.

If she fails, refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist (if you haven't already) and continue with the low-impact cardio progression below as an alternative Phase 4.

---

## PHASE 4 — Return to Running (Weeks 10–12 / 14–16 weeks postpartum)

**Goal:** Structured return to running using walk-jog progression. Maintain low-impact conditioning. Build genuine cardio fitness.

### Weekly cardio structure
- 2 walk-jog sessions
- 1 low-impact conditioning session
- 1 long walk

### Walk-Jog Progression

This is conservative on purpose. Postpartum return-to-run guidelines from pelvic health physios consistently use longer walk-to-jog ratios than general C25K programmes. She's not just untrained — she's recovering from surgery and pregnancy.

**Week 10 — Session 1 & 2 (Mon and Thu, separated by 48+ hours)**
- 5 min brisk walk warm-up
- 8 × (1 min jog at RPE 6 / 2 min walk)
- 5 min walk cool-down
- Total: ~35 min

**Week 11**
- Session 1: 5 min walk + 6 × (90 sec jog / 90 sec walk) + 5 min walk
- Session 2: 5 min walk + 5 × (2 min jog / 90 sec walk) + 5 min walk

**Week 12**
- Session 1: 5 min walk + 4 × (3 min jog / 90 sec walk) + 5 min walk
- Session 2: 5 min walk + 3 × (5 min jog / 2 min walk) + 5 min walk

### Symptom monitoring during return to run
After every jog session check:
- Any leakage during or after?
- Any pelvic heaviness or "dragging" sensation up to 24 hours after?
- Any new lower back or pelvic pain?
- How does she feel the next morning?

**If any symptom appears: drop back one week of progression and retest at that level. If symptoms persist over two sessions, stop running and refer to a pelvic floor physio.**

### Low-Impact Conditioning Session (Tuesday or Saturday)

This stays in even as she returns to running. Variety reduces impact load and maintains the aerobic engine.

| Week | Session |
|---|---|
| 10 | 30 min bike intervals: 5 min easy + 6 × (1 min hard / 2 min easy) + 5 min cool-down |
| 11 | 35 min steady state at RPE 6 (bike, incline walk, or rower if available) |
| 12 | 25 min mixed intervals: 5 min warm-up + 4 × (3 min RPE 7 / 2 min easy) + 5 min cool-down |

### Long walk (Sunday)
- 60–75 min at RPE 4. Active recovery, base maintenance, mental health.

Don't programme cardio and strength haphazardly. The schedule below balances loading and recovery.

### Phase 3 weekly template

| Day | Session |

| Monday | Strength A (lower) |
| Tuesday | Cardio steady state |
| Wednesday | Strength B (upper) |
| Thursday | Cardio intervals |
| Friday | Strength C (full body) |
| Saturday | Long walk OR optional easy bike |
| Sunday | Full rest |

### Phase 4 weekly template

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Strength A (lower) + walk-jog 1 |
| Tuesday | Low-impact conditioning |
| Wednesday | Strength B (upper) |
| Thursday | Walk-jog 2 |
| Friday | Strength C (power & full body) |
| Saturday | Long walk |

**Important:** Don't double up walk-jog with lower-body strength on different sides of the day if she's symptomatic. If Monday's combined load is too much, move walk-jog to Tuesday and shift the low-impact session.

## Cardio While Breastfeeding — Practical Notes

- **Feed before training** when possible. Engorgement during exercise is uncomfortable and breast support matters more than usual.
- **Sports bra:** invest in a high-support bra fitted for current size. Underwire is fine if it doesn't compress milk ducts. Recheck fit every 3–4 weeks.
- **Hydration:** add 500 ml of water for every 30 min of cardio on top of normal intake.
- **Timing:** longer or harder sessions early in the day if possible — energy is generally better, and recovery has time before bed.
- **Lactic acid in milk:** the old concern that exercise makes breastmilk taste sour and babies refuse it is largely overblown. Modern evidence shows minimal effect at moderate intensities. At very high intensities there's a small, temporary effect. Not a reason to avoid cardio — just feed before, not immediately after, very hard sessions if she notices baby fussiness.

## Cardio Volume and Nutrition

The nutrition plan was set at maintenance during the original Phase 3. With cardio added at this volume, that calorie target holds — don't drop it.

**On heavier cardio days** (intervals + long walk weeks):
- Add 200–300 kcal to that day, mostly carbs
- Pre-cardio snack 60 min before: banana + Greek yoghurt, oats + fruit, toast + honey + peanut butter
- Post-cardio: protein + carb recovery within an hour

**Signs cardio volume is too high:**
- Energy dropping for 3+ days running
- Milk supply decreasing (fewer wet nappies, baby fussier at breast)
- Weight loss exceeding 0.5 kg/week
- Mood crashing
- Sleep getting worse despite no change in baby's pattern

Any of these → cut cardio volume by 30% for a week and reassess.

---

## Target Cardio Capacity by Week 12

By the end of the programme she should be able to:
- Hold a brisk walk at RPE 5 for 60+ min comfortably
- Complete 5 × 2 min interval sets at RPE 7–8 without symptoms
- Jog continuously for 5 min, multiple times within a session, symptom-free
- Climb a flight of stairs without breathlessness
- Resting heart rate trending downward toward pre-pregnancy

**What comes next (post-Week 12):**
- Continue walk-jog progression toward continuous 20–30 min jogging by ~6 months postpartum
- Structured 5k programme by 7–8 months postpartum if that's her goal
- Add a 4th cardio session if running becomes the focus
- Introduce higher-intensity work (true HIIT, hill repeats, tempo runs) only after 6 months postpartum and only if pelvic floor is fully resilient

---

## The Bottom Line on Cardio

She'll feel the cardio progression more obviously than the strength progression — fitness comes back fast for someone who had a base before pregnancy. But fitness returning faster than tissue tolerance is exactly how postpartum injuries happen. Hold her back when she wants to push, particularly on impact. The walk-jog progression in Phase 4 will feel slow to her. That's correct. Run her through one return-to-run cycle properly and she's a runner again at 6 months. Rush it and she's seeing a pelvic floor physio at 4 months instead.

Pacing isn't conservatism. It's the fastest route there.

# HIIT and Postpartum — When and How

Short answer: **not in this 12-week programme.** True HIIT — maximum effort intervals at RPE 9–10 with short recovery — is too much, too soon for someone returning from a C-section while breastfeeding. The earliest she should approach genuine HIIT is **6 months postpartum**, and only with the right markers in place.

That said, "HIIT" gets used loosely. Let's separate what she's probably asking for from what the term actually means, and map out a realistic progression.

## What HIIT Actually Is (vs. What People Call HIIT)

| Term | What it is | RPE | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **True HIIT** | Max or near-max efforts, short recovery | 9–10 | 8 × 20 sec all-out / 10 sec rest (Tabata) |
| **High-intensity intervals** | Hard but submaximal, structured recovery | 7–8 | 5 × 2 min hard / 2 min easy |
| **Circuit training** | Continuous moderate-hard work, mixed exercises | 6–7 | 30 sec work / 15 sec rest, 5 stations |
| **"HIIT class" at a gym** | Usually circuit training mislabelled | 6–8 | Bootcamp, F45, Barry's |

The middle two she's already doing by Phase 4 — Thursday intervals at RPE 7–8 and Friday's circuit work are exactly this. So in practical terms, **she's already doing what most people call HIIT by Week 12.**

When clients ask about HIIT, they usually mean one of three things:
1. **"I want to feel like I'm working hard"** — already covered in Phase 3 and 4
2. **"I want short, efficient workouts"** — fair, can be programmed
3. **"I want to burn fat fast"** — the metabolic claims around HIIT vs other cardio are overhyped, especially while breastfeeding

Ask her what she actually means. The answer changes the programming.

## Why True HIIT is a Bad Bet Right Now

Specific to her situation at 4 months postpartum, breastfeeding, post-C-section:

**1. Pelvic floor load.** True HIIT typically involves jumping, sprinting, burpees, or maximal exertion — all of which spike intra-abdominal pressure. Her pelvic floor at 4 months postpartum can handle the Phase 4 intervals but is not ready for repeated max-effort impact. Stress incontinence and prolapse developed at this stage take months to resolve.

**2. C-section scar and abdominal wall.** Max-effort exhalation and impact loading stress the linea alba and scar tissue. Even with a closed diastasis, the fascia is still remodelling out to 6–12 months.

**3. Hormonal and recovery cost.** True HIIT spikes cortisol significantly. In a breastfeeding, sleep-deprived woman, that cortisol load can:
   - Suppress milk supply
   - Worsen sleep quality (already compromised)
   - Stall recovery from strength work
   - Affect mood — particularly relevant given postnatal depression risk

**4. Diminishing returns vs. cost.** The cardiovascular and metabolic benefits of true HIIT are largely available from the RPE 7–8 interval work she's already doing, at a fraction of the recovery cost. Pushing to RPE 9–10 adds marginal fitness for substantial recovery debt.

**5. Injury risk on fatigued tissue.** Connective tissue takes longer than muscle to adapt postpartum. Max-effort work on tissue that hasn't fully remodelled is how non-contact injuries happen.

## What She CAN Do Across the 12 Weeks (and What's Already Programmed)

Re-frame what's already in the plan:

- **Phase 3 Thursday intervals** at RPE 7–8 (low-impact)
- **Phase 4 Thursday walk-jog intervals**
- **Phase 4 Friday power & strength session** with plyo block
- **Phase 4 Tuesday bike intervals** at RPE 7

That's three intense sessions a week by Week 12. That is already the upper end of what she should be doing while breastfeeding and recovering.

**Adding true HIIT on top of this is not the answer. Replacing one of these with HIIT before 6 months is also not the answer.**

## The Honest Timeline for HIIT

### Months 4–6 postpartum (this programme through ~Week 20)
- **No true HIIT.**
- Highest intensity caps at RPE 8.
- Intervals are 60–120 sec work, equal or longer rest.
- Low-impact options dominate (bike, incline walk, rower).
- Plyometrics introduced in tiny doses (Phase 4 Friday).

### Months 6–9 postpartum
- **HIIT can be introduced if all green lights are present** (see below).
- Start with 1 session/week, replacing one of the existing interval sessions — not adding to volume.
- Modified HIIT first: 30 sec work / 30 sec rest, 6–8 rounds, RPE 8.
- Build to shorter recovery and higher intensity over 4–6 weeks.

### Months 9–12 postpartum
- **True HIIT formats** (Tabata, 40/20, EMOMs at high intensity) become appropriate if she's tolerated the progression.
- 1–2 sessions/week maximum.
- Still balanced with strength and steady-state cardio.

### Beyond 12 months postpartum
- Programme as you would any other client, with attention to pelvic floor symptoms long-term.
- Many women never have issues with HIIT post-recovery. Others find certain movements (high-impact jumping, heavy lifting + breath-holding) trigger symptoms even years later. Individual screening matters.

## Green Lights Required Before Introducing HIIT (Month 6+)

All of these must be in place:

**Pelvic floor and core:**
- Zero leakage during any exercise, including jumping, running, sneezing, coughing
- Zero pelvic heaviness or bulging during or after exercise
- Diastasis fully closed, no doming on any movement
- Can do 20 single-leg hops/side, 30 sec single-leg balance, full plank 60 sec without symptoms
- Sustained running for 20+ min without symptoms

**Recovery capacity:**
- Sleeping at least one stretch of 4–5 hours per night (most nights)
- Energy consistently 7+/10
- Recovering from current Phase 4 sessions within 24–48 hours
- No persistent muscle soreness lasting 3+ days

**Breastfeeding context:**
- Milk supply robust and not on a downward trend
- Either solids well-established (around 6 months) so feeding demands are reducing, or she's confident in supply with current training load

**Other:**
- C-section scar fully healed, mobile, no pulling
- No back, hip, or pelvic pain
- Nutrition supports current training (not in a meaningful deficit)
- Mental health stable

**Missing any of these → not yet.** The cost is too high relative to the benefit.

## If She Wants Short, Hard Sessions Now — Programming Alternatives

These give her the "feeling" of HIIT without the postpartum risk. All appropriate to introduce in Phase 4 (Week 10+) of the current programme as occasional substitutions for the Friday session.

### Option 1 — Low-impact metabolic circuit (20 min)
3 rounds, 40 sec work / 20 sec rest:
- Goblet squat
- Incline push-up
- DB Romanian deadlift
- Band row
- Bear hold or dead bug

RPE 7. No jumping. Strength patterns under fatigue.

### Option 2 — Bike sprints (20 min)
- 5 min warm-up
- 8 × (30 sec hard / 90 sec easy)
- 5 min cool-down

RPE 8 on the hard intervals. Bike removes pelvic floor impact load.

### Option 3 — Strength density block (25 min)
EMOM (every minute on the minute) for 20 min:
- Min 1: 8 goblet squats
- Min 2: 8 push-ups
- Min 3: 8 DB rows
- Min 4: 30 sec bear hold
- Repeat × 5

RPE 7. Density gives the metabolic effect without max effort.

### Option 4 — Hill walking intervals
- 5 min flat warm-up
- 6 × (90 sec steep incline at RPE 7–8 / 90 sec flat recovery)
- 5 min cool-down

Max intensity without impact. Excellent stimulus.

**Any of these can substitute for Phase 4 Session C occasionally. Don't add them on top of the existing programme.**

## What to Tell Her

Three things to communicate clearly:

**1. "You're already doing the work."** By Week 12 she has three high-intensity sessions a week. The marginal benefit of pushing harder is small. The cost — pelvic floor symptoms, milk supply, recovery — is large.

**2. "HIIT will be there in two months."** Frame it as a milestone, not a denial. Around Month 6, with the green lights in place, true HIIT becomes appropriate. She's not being held back forever — she's being protected from a setback.

**3. "Intensity isn't the same as effectiveness."** The thing she's chasing — feeling strong, looking the way she wants, having her energy back — is being built right now through strength progression, steady cardio, structured intervals, and nutrition. HIIT is one tool, and not the most important one at this stage.

If she's frustrated, that's reasonable. She's been through a major surgery and pregnancy, she's caring for a newborn, she's working hard in the gym, and she wants to feel like an athlete again. The answer isn't to push her into true HIIT — it's to make sure she sees the gains from what's already programmed. By Week 12 she'll be doing things she couldn't do at Week 6. That's the win. HIIT is the next chapter, not this one.

## The Bottom Line

**No true HIIT in this 12-week programme.** The Phase 4 interval and circuit work delivers most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost. Earliest reasonable introduction is Month 6 postpartum with full green lights. The right move now is to nail the existing programme and protect her ability to train hard for the next decade — not to chase intensity that her tissue isn't ready for.

If she pushes back, that's the conversation: "I'm not saying no forever. I'm saying not yet, and here's exactly when and how we add it." Most clients accept that when they understand the reasoning.

# Complete 12-Week Postpartum Return Programme

**Client profile:** 33-year-old female, 4 weeks post uncomplicated C-section, breastfeeding, OB-cleared for light activity only until 6-week check-up. Training environment: home, yoga mat only at programme start; resistance bands and adjustable dumbbells added by Week 6.

**Goal:** Return to strength, cardiovascular fitness, and core function. Client wants to feel strong by Week 12.

---

## Programme-Wide Caveats

- **OB clearance required at the 6-week check before progressing past Phase 1.** If clearance is delayed or restricted, hold at Phase 1.
- **Screen for diastasis recti** at Week 5, then every 3–4 weeks. >3 fingers or soft/squishy at any width → refer to pelvic floor physiotherapist before progressing flexion-based core work.
- **Pelvic floor physio referral early is strongly recommended.** Many of the screening and progression decisions are easier with a specialist already involved.
- **C-section scar:** any pulling, sharp pain, redness, or discharge → stop and refer to her doctor. Scar mobilisation can begin once fully healed and signed off (usually 6–8 weeks).
- **Stop-immediately symptoms:** return of heavy bleeding, pelvic heaviness or bulging, urinary leakage, abdominal doming, scar pain.
- **Sleep, feeding, and emotional state drive intensity more than the programme does.** Build flexibility in. Bad night = swap a session for a walk and breathwork.
- **Mental health check-ins:** postnatal depression affects ~1 in 7. Refer to GP if mood, motivation, or affect concerns you. Not a training problem.
- **No true HIIT in this 12-week programme.** Earliest reasonable introduction is Month 6 postpartum with full green lights present.

---

## Equipment Recommendations

**Phase 1–2:** yoga mat only.

**Before Week 6, acquire (in priority order):**
1. Resistance bands — loop set (light/medium/heavy) + long tube band with handles + door anchor (~£20–35)
2. Adjustable dumbbells, 2–24 kg range (~£100–200), or pairs of 5 / 8 / 12 kg
3. Backpack loaded with books/rice for carries and squats (free)
4. Sturdy chair or sofa for split squats, step-ups, incline push-ups (she has)

If only one purchase possible: bands + door anchor. If two: add dumbbells.

# PHASE 1 — Foundation & Reconnection
## Weeks 1–2 of programme / Weeks 4–6 postpartum

**Goal:** Gentle reactivation of breath, pelvic floor, and deep core. Walking volume. No abdominal flexion, no loaded movement, no impact.

### Week 1

**Walking:** 15–20 min daily if tolerated, flat, conversational pace (RPE 3).

**Daily breath & floor session (10 min):**
- Diaphragmatic breathing, supine knees bent — 5 min, slow nasal inhale 360° ribs, long exhale
- Pelvic floor connection on exhale — 2 × 10 slow contractions, full release between
- Supported side-lying rest with deep breathing — 3 min

### Week 2

**Walking:** 20–30 min daily, with one 35 min walk on a good day. RPE 3–4.

**Daily session (12–15 min):**
- Diaphragmatic breathing — 3 min
- Pelvic floor: 2 × 10 slow holds (3–5 sec) + 2 × 10 quick flicks
- Supine pelvic tilts — 2 × 10
- Glute bridges, exhale up — 2 × 8
- Cat-cow — 2 × 8

**END OF WEEK 2 — 6-WEEK OB CHECK. Do not progress without clearance.**

# PHASE 2 — Rebuild Foundations
## Weeks 3–5 of programme / Weeks 7–9 postpartum

**Goal:** Reintroduce light strength, bodyweight only. Extend cardio duration. No crunches, no planks, no impact.

### Weekly Structure
- 3 strength sessions (25–30 min) — Mon/Wed/Fri
- 4 walks (30–45 min) + 1 longer walk (45–60 min)
- Daily floor/breath work (5 min)
- 1 full rest day

### Diastasis Screen at End of Week 5
Supine, knees bent. Lift head slightly. Palpate horizontally 2 cm above navel, at navel, 2 cm below.
- **<2 fingers, firm:** progress to Phase 3
- **2–3 fingers, firm:** progress cautiously
- **>3 fingers OR soft/squishy:** refer to pelvic floor physio before progressing

### Strength Session (M/W/F)

Warm-up: cat-cow ×8, glute bridge ×10, diaphragmatic breath ×5

| Exercise | Week 3 | Week 4 | Week 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Glute bridge | 3 × 10 | 3 × 10, 2-sec hold | Single-leg, 3 × 6/side |
| Bodyweight squat to chair | 3 × 10 | 3 × 12 | 3 × 15 |
| Bird dog | 3 × 6/side | 3 × 8/side | 3 × 8/side, 2-sec hold |
| Wall push-up | 3 × 8 | 3 × 10 | Incline push-up (sofa) 3 × 8 |

| Clamshell side-lying | 2 × 10/side | + side-lying leg lifts 2 × 10/side | Clamshell with pulse 2 × 12/side |

**Cue throughout:** "Connect, then move." Exhale before initiating movement with gentle pelvic floor lift and lower abdominal draw-in.

### Cardio (Walks)

| Week | Walks | Long walk | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 4 × 30–35 min @ RPE 4 | 45 min @ RPE 4 | Add gentle incline on one walk |
| 4 | 4 × 35–40 min @ RPE 4–5 | 50 min @ RPE 4 | Pace play: 2 min normal / 1 min brisk × 5 |
| 5 | 4 × 40 min @ RPE 5 | 55–60 min @ RPE 4 | Pace play: 4 min normal / 2 min brisk × 5 |

**Low-impact alternatives if available:** stationary bike 25–35 min @ RPE 5; swimming 20–30 min easy (only after OB check, lochia fully stopped, no infection).

# PHASE 3 — Build Strength & Capacity (Intensity Push)
## Weeks 6–9 of programme / Weeks 10–13 postpartum

**Goal:** Drive genuine strength and aerobic capacity. Prepare for impact reintroduction. She wants to feel strong by Week 12 — this is where we lay that foundation.

### Green-Light Criteria Before Pushing Intensity

All must be true at start of Week 6:
- Diastasis closed to <2 fingers, firm, no doming
- No pelvic floor symptoms (no leakage, heaviness, bulging)
- C-section scar fully healed, mobile, no pulling
- Sleep averaging 5+ hours total per night (broken is fine)
- Energy 6+/10 most days
- Milk supply stable
- Phase 2 sessions completed without symptom flare
- Nutrition at maintenance, not deficit

If any are off, run a moderated version of Phase 3 — drop the loading guidance by one level and skip Session D.

### Weekly Structure

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Strength A — Lower Body |
| Tuesday | Cardio — Steady State |
| Wednesday | Strength B — Upper Body & Posterior |
| Thursday | Cardio — Intervals |
| Friday | Strength C — Full Body |
| Saturday | Long walk OR Optional Session D |
| Sunday | Full rest |

**Rest periods:** 90 sec on main lifts, 45–60 sec on accessories.
**RPE targets:** main lifts at RPE 7–8 by Week 8 (2–3 reps in tank).

### Strength Session A — Lower Body (Monday)

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Tempo / Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Goblet squat | 4 × 8 | 3-sec lowering, 1-sec pause bottom |
| DB Romanian deadlift | 4 × 8 | 3-sec lowering |
| Reverse lunge (DBs) | 3 × 8/side | Controlled, no momentum |
| Single-leg glute bridge | 3 × 10/side | 2-sec hold at top |
| Suitcase carry (heavy) | 3 × 40 sec/side | Anti-lateral flexion |
| Side plank, full | 3 × 25–30 sec/side | Add hip dip if easy |

### Strength Session B — Upper & Posterior (Wednesday)

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Tempo / Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Push-up (lowest incline she can manage clean) | 4 × 6–8 | 3-sec lowering |
| Single-arm DB row | 4 × 8/side | 1-sec squeeze at top |
| DB shoulder press, standing | 4 × 8 | Brace hard, no back arch |
| DB floor press | 3 × 10 | Horizontal pressing |
| Band pull-apart + face pull superset | 3 × 15 each | Posture and rear delt |
| Dead bug full + Pallof press superset | 3 × 8/side each | Anti-extension + anti-rotation |

### Strength Session C — Full Body Density (Friday)

**Pair 1 (3 rounds, 60 sec rest after both):**
- Goblet squat × 8, 3-sec lowering
- Single-arm DB row × 10/side

**Pair 2 (3 rounds):**
- DB Romanian deadlift × 8
- Incline push-up × 8, 3-sec lowering

**Pair 3 (3 rounds):**
- Bulgarian split squat × 6/side
- DB shoulder press × 8

**Finisher (1 round, hard):**
- Bear crawl hold × 30 sec
- Side plank × 30 sec/side
- Hollow body hold, regressed × 20 sec

### Optional Session D — Posterior Chain & Carries (Saturday)

Add only if Weeks 6–7 have gone smoothly. Skip if fatigued.

- Hip thrust off sofa (DB on hips) — 4 × 10
- Single-leg RDL — 3 × 8/side
- Glute bridge with band, slow tempo — 3 × 15
- Farmer's carry — 4 × 40 sec
- Bird dog with 3-sec hold — 3 × 10/side
- Dead bug with band-resisted arms — 3 × 10/side

### Cardio Session 1 — Steady State (Tuesday)

| Week | Session | RPE |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 35 min brisk walk with rolling incline | 5–6 |
| 7 | 40 min brisk walk with incline OR 30 min bike | 6 |
| 8 | 45 min brisk walk with incline OR 35 min bike | 6 |
| 9 | 30 min sustained effort | 6–7 |

### Cardio Session 2 — Intervals (Thursday)

Low-impact only (incline walking, bike, hill walking, stair climbing).

| Week | Session |
|---|---|
| 6 | 5 min warm-up + 6 × (1 min RPE 7 / 2 min RPE 4) + 5 min cool-down |
| 7 | 5 min warm-up + 8 × (1 min RPE 7 / 90 sec RPE 4) + 5 min cool-down |
| 8 | 5 min warm-up + 6 × (90 sec RPE 7–8 / 90 sec RPE 4) + 5 min cool-down |
| 9 | 5 min warm-up + 5 × (2 min RPE 7–8 / 2 min RPE 4) + 5 min cool-down |

### Long Walk (Saturday or Sunday)
60–75 min at RPE 4. Base building, recovery, mental health. Pram-pushing fine.

### Week-by-Week Strength Progression

**Week 6 — Calibration**
Find working loads at new rep ranges. Goblet squat RPE 7 by final set of 8. Starting loads: squat 12–14 kg, RDL 2 × 8–10 kg, row 8–10 kg, press 2 × 5–7 kg. Tempo work in from day 1. **No Session D this week.**

**Week 7 — Load**
Add weight where Week 6 finished with reps in tank. Squat 14–16 kg, RDL 2 × 10–12 kg, row 10–12 kg. Same rep schemes. Optional Session D if recovery allows.

**Week 8 — Density & volume**
Loads hold from Week 7. Reduce rest periods by 15 sec. Add a set on main lifts: Squat 5 × 8, RDL 5 × 8, Row 5 × 8. Hardest week of the block.

**Week 9 — Peak & test**
Loads up: squat 16–20 kg, RDL 2 × 12–14 kg. Drop to 4 × 8 (lower volume, heavier).

**End-of-Week-9 test session** (replace Session C):
- Goblet squat: top set of 6 at RPE 8
- Push-up: max unbroken reps with good form
- Single-arm DB row: heaviest 8 reps/side
- Side plank: longest hold/side
- Suitcase carry: heaviest 40 sec/side

Document everything. These numbers carry into Phase 4.

### Phase 3 Target Numbers by End of Week 9

| Lift | Target |
|---|---|
| Goblet squat | 18–22 kg × 6 |
| DB RDL | 2 × 14–16 kg × 8 |
| DB row | 14–18 kg × 8/side |
| DB shoulder press | 2 × 7–10 kg × 8 |
| Push-up | full or low-incline × 6–8 |
| Side plank | 35–40 sec/side |
| Suitcase carry | 16–20 kg × 40 sec/side |

### Impact-Readiness Check — End of Week 9

Before Phase 4 jogging she must pass all:
- No leakage during exertion or cough/sneeze
- No pelvic heaviness or bulging
- Single-leg balance × 30 sec each side
- Single-leg glute bridge × 20 reps/side
- Walking lunge with control
- 1 min jogging on the spot — symptom-free
- 10 single-leg hops/side — symptom-free
- 20 jumping jacks — symptom-free

**Fail any → no impact yet.** Continue Phase 4 strength as written, replace walk-jog with bike intervals and hill walking. Refer to pelvic health physio if you haven't already.

### Diastasis Re-check at End of Week 8
Required before reintroducing flexion-based core work in Phase 4.

# PHASE 4 — Reintroduce Impact & Build Strength
## Weeks 10–12 of programme / Weeks 14–16 postpartum

**Goal:** Return to impact, push genuine strength, reintroduce controlled flexion-based core. By Week 12 she feels strong, confident, and ready for the next block.

### Weekly Structure

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Strength A (lower) + walk-jog 1 |
| Tuesday | Low-impact conditioning |
| Wednesday | Strength B (upper) |
| Thursday | Walk-jog 2 |
| Friday | Strength C (power & full body) |
| Saturday | Long walk |
| Sunday | Full rest |

If Monday's combined load is too much, move walk-jog to Tuesday and shift low-impact session.

### Strength Session A — Lower Body Strength (Monday)

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Loading |
|---|---|---|
| Goblet squat | 4 × 8 | Heavier — RPE 7 |
| DB Romanian deadlift | 4 × 8 | Heaviest available |
| Bulgarian split squat | 3 × 8/side | DBs at sides |
| Hip thrust off sofa (DB on hips) | 3 × 10 | Squeeze at top |
| Suitcase carry | 3 × 30 sec/side | Heavy |
| Side plank with hip dip | 3 × 8/side | Full position |

| Exercise | Sets × Reps | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Push-up (full or knees) | 4 × 6–10 | Progress from knee to full this phase |
| Single-arm DB row | 4 × 8/side | Heavier than Phase 3 |
